summaries.example: Imagine you borrow a friend’s scooter. You are obligated to return it by noon. Returning it on time is your duty. Adding a small thank-you note might be kind, but it may be more than your duty. Deontic logic helps us ask what follows from words such as “must,” “may,” and “must not.”
summaries.summary: Deontic logic is the study of reasoning about norms: rules about what people must do, may do, or must not do. It examines concepts such as obligation, permission, prohibition, and optional action. For example, if you must return a borrowed scooter, then failing to return it is forbidden. You might also be allowed to return it with extra care, without being required to do so. The subject asks which conclusions follow from these statements. It grew partly from modal logic, which studies necessity and possibility. The comparison is useful because “obligatory” can resemble “necessary,” while “permissible” can resemble “possible.” But the comparison has limits. A necessary truth cannot fail to be true, while a duty can be broken. Deontic logic therefore develops formal systems that resemble modal logic while handling the special features of rules and responsibilities. The entry also explains that ordinary language contains more distinctions than a simple system may express, including doing the least one can do, going beyond duty, acting as an agent, and dealing with conditional duties. Its central lesson is that reasoning about norms is useful but difficult: small changes in how we understand “ought” or “may” can change what conclusions a system allows.
key_ideas: Deontic logic studies reasoning about duties and permissions.
A duty can be broken. Saying something is required does not mean it always happens.
Permission, prohibition, and optionality are related, but they are not always the same idea in everyday language.
Early deontic logic compared duties with modal ideas such as necessity and possibility.
Formal systems use symbols and rules to test whether conclusions really follow.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use rules in families, schools, organizations, laws, and computer systems. Deontic logic gives us a careful way to check whether a conclusion really follows from rules. It also shows why everyday words such as “must,” “ought,” and “may” can be trickier than they first seem.

important_terms.definition: A branch of logic that studies how ideas about duties, permissions, and prohibitions affect what follows from what.
Something that is required or is your duty.
Something you are allowed to do.
Something that is not allowed.
Something that is not required, so you may do it or leave it undone.
A logic about necessity and possibility, such as whether something must be true or could be true.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be a duty even when a person fails to do it?
Is every action that is not forbidden truly optional?
Why might permission and “doing nothing wrong” feel different?
What rules should a logic use when two duties conflict?

summaries.example: Suppose a school rule says that a student must submit an assignment by Friday. A second rule says that if the student submits it, the student ought to include a source list. What if the student misses Friday? One system may still treat the source-list requirement as connected to the original duty; another may treat it as applying only in the ideal case where the assignment is submitted. This kind of problem motivates the study of conditional obligations and competing forms of inference.
summaries.summary: Deontic logic studies the inferential behavior of normative notions. Its traditional starting point treats obligation as a basic operator and defines related statuses: permission, prohibition, omission, optionality, and non-optionality. These definitions create a pattern analogous to the modal pattern involving necessity, possibility, and impossibility. The analogy is illuminating but imperfect. Alethic necessity is truth-implicating: what is necessary is true. An obligation, by contrast, can be violated, so “obligatory” cannot simply mean “necessarily true.” Standard Deontic Logic, or SDL, is a benchmark system. It combines classical propositional logic with a normal modal-style obligation operator and a no-conflict principle. Its possible-worlds semantics evaluates an obligation at a world by examining the worlds acceptable from that standpoint: a proposition is obligatory when it holds at all such worlds, and permissible when it holds at at least one. This framework explains many traditional relationships, but it also generates controversial consequences. For instance, logical weakening can turn an obligation to mail a letter into an apparent obligation to mail it or burn it. Conditional obligations create a deeper challenge. In a famous pattern, a person has a primary duty, a duty conditional on fulfilling it, a contrary-to-duty requirement if it is violated, and a fact reporting the violation. A simple material-conditional treatment can produce contradiction or destroy the independence of the claims. Researchers therefore disagree about whether factual or deontic detachment should govern such cases, and about whether conditional obligations should be treated as composites or as primitive relations. Later work enriches or revises SDL to handle agency, temporal order
key_ideas: The traditional scheme defines several normative statuses from obligation, including permission, prohibition, omission, optionality, and non-optionality.
Deontic and alethic modal systems have formal similarities, but obligations are violable, so obligation does not imply actual truth.
SDL uses classical logic, a normal modal-style rule, and a principle excluding simultaneous obligations to do and not do the same thing.
Possible-worlds semantics interprets obligation by looking at worlds acceptable from the standpoint of a given world.
Conditional obligations expose limits of simple unary systems: different ways of handling conditional reasoning support different kinds of detachment.
The entry surveys extensions for agency, time, normative gaps, supererogation, conflicts, and weaker or non-classical systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Normative reasoning appears in ethics, law, organizations, security systems, and computer applications. Formalizing it can reveal hidden assumptions: whether every unrequired act is indifferent, whether duties can conflict, and whether an obligation concerns a state of affairs or an agent’s action. Deontic logic matters not because one system has settled every issue, but because its formal models make disagreements precise.

important_terms.definition: A formal study of how normative concepts—such as obligation, permission, prohibition, and what is beyond duty—contribute to inference.
A modal notion concerning what must be true or could be true, rather than what is required by a norm.
The idea that a statement is required; in standard systems it is often represented by a one-place obligation operator.
The status of being allowed. In traditional systems it is often defined as the failure of the negation to be obligatory.
A standard normal modal system used as a benchmark in deontic logic, with obligation as its basic operator and a no-conflict principle.
A semantic framework that evaluates formulas at worlds and uses a relation to identify worlds acceptable or accessible from a given world.
A duty that applies when another duty has been violated, such as what should be done if a primary requirement is not met.
An action that is allowed and goes beyond what duty requires; standard systems often struggle to represent this distinction.

questions_to_think_about: Should an obligation to do something imply that the action is possible?
Should a duty to mail a letter imply a duty to mail it or burn it?
When a primary duty is violated, should a related conditional duty still be detachable?
Can a formal system represent both optionality and the difference between ordinary and morally better choices?
Should conflicting obligations make every conclusion follow, or should a logic tolerate the conflict?

summaries.example: A community club has this rule: members must return borrowed equipment on time. It also says that if someone returns equipment, they should clean it first. One member returns it late and dirty. Does the cleaning rule still apply? A simple logic may give an answer that creates trouble. Deontic logicians study different ways to represent the rules so that the result matches—or clearly challenges—our ordinary reasoning.
summaries.summary: Deontic logic is a branch of logic concerned with normative language. It studies how statements about what is obligatory, permissible, forbidden, optional, or beyond duty contribute to reasoning. A basic example is the difference between returning a borrowed item on time, which may be required, and doing an extra kindness, which may be praiseworthy without being required. The subject began by comparing normative concepts with modal concepts. In modal logic, necessity and possibility describe how things must or could be. In deontic logic, obligation and permission can be arranged in similar patterns. Yet the comparison has an important limit: a necessary truth cannot be false, whereas an obligation can be violated. Standard Deontic Logic, often called SDL, uses a formal obligation operator and rules inherited from normal modal logic. In its possible-worlds interpretation, the acceptable worlds related to a situation are used to test a norm. A claim is obligatory if it holds in every relevant acceptable world; it is permitted if it holds in at least one. This approach captures many useful relationships, but it also creates puzzles. Logical reasoning may make it appear that an obligation to do one thing includes an obligation to do that thing or something forbidden. Another major problem concerns conditional obligations. A person may have a primary duty, a requirement that applies if the duty is fulfilled, and a different requirement that applies if it is violated. Translating all these claims with one simple operator can produce contradiction or lose the distinctions between them. Deontic logicians therefore develop competing extensions and alternatives. key_ideas: Deontic logic asks not only what rules say, but what follows from those rules.
The traditional approach connects obligation with permission and prohibition through formal definitions.
The analogy between obligation and necessity is helpful, but it cannot be exact because obligations can be violated.
Standard Deontic Logic uses possible worlds: acceptable worlds help determine what is obligatory or permitted.
Conditional duties are difficult because a duty can depend on whether another action happens or fails to happen.
Different systems try to represent extra ideas, such as agency, legal gaps, exceptional duties, and conflicts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rules guide behavior in classrooms, clubs, laws, workplaces, and software. Deontic logic helps us examine whether a rule system is consistent and whether a conclusion is really supported. It also teaches caution: ordinary words such as “ought,” “must,” and “may” can carry different meanings, and a formal system may capture some meanings while missing others.

important_terms.definition: The study of how rules about what is required, allowed, or forbidden affect logical conclusions.
A requirement or duty, even though people may fail to carry it out.
An action or state of affairs that the rules allow.
An action or state of affairs that the rules forbid.
A situation in which something and its opposite are both not required; it may be done or left undone.
A model of logic that studies necessity, possibility, and related ideas.
A benchmark system that treats obligation like a modal operator and includes a rule against conflicting obligations.
A requirement that applies after an earlier duty has not been fulfilled.

questions_to_think_about: If a rule permits an action, does that mean it is morally indifferent?
If you are required to help, are you also required to help or do something harmful?
What should a logic say when two promises create opposite duties?
Does a conditional duty still matter after its condition is not met?
Should “ought to be true” and “ought to do” be represented in the same way?
